title: Chance Decides Which Stem Cell Wins

scenes.tts: The lining of a mouse's small intestine is replaced every few days. Yet the animal keeps that lining for life. Cells are born in a pocket called a crypt. They move up and are shed at the tip. Something at the bottom of each crypt never runs out. Which cells are they, and how would you prove it?
scenes.visual: A crypt outline; grey cells stream up and are shed at the tip; a dashed ring with a question mark circles the base cells.
scenes.narration: The lining of a mouse's small intestine is replaced every few days. Yet the animal keeps that lining for life. Cells are born in a pocket called a crypt. They move up and are shed at the tip. Something at the bottom of each crypt never runs out. Which cells are they, and how would you prove it?

scenes.tts: Expressing a gene tells you nothing about fate. So scientists trace cells instead. A drug called tamoxifen switches on a permanent mark in a cell at the crypt base. Every daughter cell inherits that mark. Over sixty days, the label filled ribbons of epithelium. Those ribbons contained every kind of epithelial cell. That shows multipotency within the gut. It does not show pluripotency.
scenes.visual: One base cell turns green when tamoxifen arrives; a green ribbon rises among unlabelled cells over a 60 day bar; chips say multipotent within the gut, and a crossed-out chip says pluripotent.

scenes.tts: How do the stem cells share the crypt? One cartoon says each stem cell divides unevenly, every time. One stem cell, and one short-lived cell. In 2010, Hugo Snippert and colleagues tested it. Their reporter gives each clone a random colour, one of four. These stem cells divide about once a day. Most divisions were symmetric, giving two stem cells or two non-stem cells.
scenes.visual: Left: the always-uneven division cartoon. A plain cell picks one of four colours. Right: the two symmetric outcomes, with a once-a-day clock.

scenes.tts: Then they waited. Over one to six months, crypts drifted toward a single colour. Surviving clones grew, while others vanished. This pattern is called neutral drift. Equivalent stem cells crowd one another out at random. Chance, not a fixed hierarchy, decides which lineage wins.
scenes.visual: A model crypt of five stem cells in different colours; one by one a cell is replaced by a copy of its neighbour until the whole crypt is one colour.

scenes.tts: Now the arithmetic, with round numbers. Label one stem cell in each of one hundred crypts. Say each crypt holds five equivalent stem cells. A labelled clone takes over its crypt with probability one in five. So expect twenty fully labelled crypts. The other eighty clones are lost. Check the count. One hundred labelled cells at the start. Twenty crypts times five cells makes one hundred at the end.

A labelled clone takes over its crypt with probability 1 in 5. So expect 20 fully labelled crypts. The other 80 clones are lost. Check the count. 100 labelled cells at the start. 20 crypts times 5 cells makes 100 at the end.
scenes.visual: A 10 by 10 grid of crypts, each with one green cell among five. Twenty crypts turn fully green, eighty lose the label. The sums 100 and 20 times 5 appear.
scenes.narration: Now the arithmetic, with round numbers. Label one stem cell in each of 100 crypts. Say each crypt holds five equivalent stem cells. Check the count. 100 labelled cells at the start. 20 crypts times 5 cells makes 100 at the end.

scenes.tts: Change five to fourteen, and the expected count drops to about seven crypts. Fourteen is roughly the number of L G R five high cells counted per crypt in the mouse small intestine. Five was an effective number for the model, smaller than that count. So counting fully labelled crypts estimates how many cells really compete. Balance is kept by the population, not by each division.
